title: The Hidden Cost of Power Outages: What Florida Businesses Lose Every Storm Season
excerpt: Power outages cost the U.S. economy an estimated $150 billion a year, and Southeast states carry a disproportionate share. Here's what that costs a Florida business, storm season after storm season.

content.text: The cost of a power outage rarely shows up as a single line item. It shows up as spoiled inventory, missed orders, idle staff, emergency equipment rentals, and - often - customers who don't come back. Add those up across a storm season, and the number is larger than most Florida businesses have actually calculated.
Here's what the data says about what an outage really costs and why Florida businesses carry more of that cost than most.
The National Numbers Are Already Staggering

A 2026 analysis from Oak Ridge National Laboratory gives the clearest picture of the trend: Major power outages cost U.S. customers an average of $67 billion a year over the past seven years, but that burden has climbed sharply, with the price tag hitting $121 billion in 2024 alone. The average cost per outage for commercial and industrial customers was $6,031 that year. Between 2018 and 2024, the number of major outages nationwide rose 29%, and the average outage length grew from 9.6 hours to 11.8 hours.

links.text: 2026 analysis from Oak Ridge National Laboratory

content.text: Those are national figures. The Oak Ridge analysis specifically noted that the highest outage costs per customer are concentrated in the Southeast and along the coasts - not coincidentally, the same regions where hurricanes do the most damage.
What That Looks Like at the Business Level

To see what that looks like for an individual business, Florida Power & Light's own reported reliability data - run through Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's Interruption Cost Estimate model - puts the average cost of a routine, non-storm power interruption at $2,955.66 for a non-residential customer, or roughly $53 for every minute the power stays off. That's the cost of an ordinary outage.

links.text: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's Interruption Cost Estimate model

content.text: A hurricane is not an ordinary outage: in 2022, Florida customers averaged 19.1 hours without power over the course of the year, the highest of any U.S. state, driven by Hurricane Ian alone leaving 2.6 million Florida customers in the dark, some for more than two weeks. Two years later, Hurricane Milton knocked out power to 3.4 million Florida customers, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Multiply an ordinary outage's per-minute cost by a multi-day hurricane restoration timeline, and the routine number stops looking routine.

content.text: The Outage Is Rarely the Whole Story

The financial exposure doesn't end when the power comes back on. FEMA has long estimated that 40% to 60% of businesses affected by a major disaster never reopen - a widely cited figure driven as much by lost data, lost customers, and depleted cash reserves as by the physical damage itself. That risk compounds with confidence: A 2026 U.S. Chamber of Commerce Foundation survey found that 94% of small business owners believe they could recover from a disaster, but only 31% actually have a plan in place.

links.text: 2026 U.S. Chamber of Commerce Foundation survey

content.text: The businesses hit hardest tend to be the ones who assumed they were the exception. That statistic is the real argument for treating backup power as a continuity investment rather than an insurance line item nobody expects to use.

None of this cost is inevitable; it's what happens when a business can't stay open before, during, and after a storm.
